A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LiMVAM research, with identifiable continuity in the ICA methods, proofs and MEG experiments. Text, equations, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

before.justification: v1 Section 6 and Appendix B report original synthetic recovery experiments, Cam-CAN MEG causal graphs and resampling-based stability results.

after.justification: v3 Section 6 and Appendix H report original simulations, runtime and assumption-sensitivity experiments, and MEG and fMRI analyses.

M1.justification: v1 centers on the Shared-ICA-based MICaDo algorithm. v3 adds PairwiseLiMVAM and DirectLiMVAM, which recursively order variables using likelihood or cross-covariance criteria and estimate coefficients through feasible generalized least squares. It also generalizes shared disturbances from s+n^i to D^i s+n^i and revises ICA scaling steps.

E1.justification: v3 retains Cam-CAN sensorimotor MEG and synthetic causal recovery, but adds an fMRI rhyming task with nine participants and nine variables. It also evaluates synthetic scenarios outside the shared-disturbance construction, including mixed sub-Gaussian, Gaussian and super-Gaussian disturbances (Section 6 and Appendix H.1.2).

E2.justification: ICA-LiNGAM and MultiGroupDirectLiNGAM remain, alongside the renamed and revised MICaDo-ML/J lineage, ICA-LiMVAM-ML/J. The MVICA-backed variant compared in v1 Figures 4–5 disappears. v3 compares its two new algorithms alongside this largely retained comparison set; Chen et al. is associated with the ICA approach rather than a separately plotted baseline.

E3.justification: The retained sample-size experiment now draws diagonal disturbance scalings uniformly between 0.1 and 3 and drops the T^i error metric. v3 introduces runtime, dimensionality and assumption-testing protocols. MEG stability resampling changes from 49 to 30 participants, while the 98-participant cohort and preprocessing are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds explicit tests of scaled-noise diversity and connectivity assumptions, plus sensitivity to numbers of views and variables (Appendix H.1.2–H.1.4). v1's noise-level sweep and view-specific-ordering sample-size sweep are removed. MEG stability analysis expands to compare PairwiseLiMVAM with ICA-LiMVAM; the original six ICA brain maps are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 50 seeds for the main simulation and 50 MEG resamples. v3 explicitly defines medians and 25th/75th-percentile error bars for Figure 5, whereas v1's plotted bands are unspecified. New experiments report 200 random runs and 30 repetitions; these do not establish increased repetitions of the original experiments.

E6.justification: v3 reports new algorithm rankings, runtime and assumption-sensitivity results, and fMRI causal edges. Mean MEG Pearson correlations between median effect matrices are 0.67 for PairwiseLiMVAM and 0.27 for ICA-LiMVAM under 30-participant resampling; v1 reports 0.39 for MICaDo under 49-participant resampling. These are different conditions, not direct cross-version performance changes.

T1.justification: v3 adds SOS criterion derivations, positivity conditions, recursive-ordering consistency arguments and new identifiability results (Appendices B–E). The original ICA theory is generalized to diagonal disturbance scalings, with view-specific ordering retained in Appendix F.3. The whole-vector independence used in Appendix C is not explicitly supplied by the within-view independence stated in Section 3.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes identifiability through Shared ICA and the MICaDo estimator. v3 centers its contributions on two new efficient SOS algorithms and consistency under more general cross-view correlation conditions, while reframing the ICA approach relative to Chen et al. Gaussian identifiability remains central, but the claimed algorithmic novelty and theoretical scope expand substantially.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations of correlation diversity, arbitrary scaling restrictions in the original shared-disturbance construction, and failures when ICA assumptions are violated. It adds comparative MEG stability and fMRI interpretations. v1's noise-level failure discussion and proposed equal-B variant for limited data are removed; existing interhemispheric MEG interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies detailed empirical criterion estimators, FGLS instructions and pseudocode, and identifies the Hungarian assignment and LiNGAM ordering heuristic. It reports MEG execution taking 2 hours 20 minutes on 5 CPUs and adds an fMRI data-access pointer. However, v1's explicit experiment-code and implementation-library links disappear despite v3's open-source claim.

R1.justification: v3 introduces Chen et al. (2024) as central prior work and acknowledges essentially equivalent ICA adjacency estimates, repositioning novelty around scaling, identifiability and the new recursive methods. v1 lacks this comparison and primarily contrasts Shimizu's multigroup approach. Regression and fMRI references are added, while the MVICA reference is removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, background and discussion are substantially rewritten. v3 organizes the main narrative around two estimation families with accompanying theory, replacing v1's separate identifiability and estimation sections. MEG preprocessing and existing theoretical material move into reorganized topical appendices, and MICaDo becomes ICA-LiMVAM.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from nine panels to six, with revised legends and removal of the T^i error row. v3 adds runtime, assumption, dimensionality and sparsity displays and a combined MEG/fMRI figure. The original noise sweep and ordering-correlation displays disappear; the MEG time series and six ICA brain maps remain as Figures 8 and 10.

improvement.justification: v3 adds substantive algorithms, broader empirical validation and useful assumption tests. However, its central new SOS guarantee has an unresolved scope issue: Section 3 states within-view independence, whereas Appendix C, including Eq. 90, requires independence between entire cross-view regressor and residual vectors. v1's shared-disturbance construction supplied that structure. This uncertainty about the expanded theoretical claims, together with the loss of explicit experiment-code access information, prevents a reliable net quality judgment despite the empirical additions.
